title: Effect of protein supplementation on hip bone mineral density, cortical thickness, and bone strength in older adult participants during a caloric restriction and aerobic exercise weight loss intervention: a randomized controlled trial

sections.abstract:
Weight loss in older age can cause bone loss. In older adults with overweight/obesity in a weight loss trial, 6-month hip bone strength increased with higher protein intake versus controls consuming the Recommended Dietary Allowance. However, greater weight loss was associated with greater 18-month hip bone mineral density loss.

Weight loss (WL) to treat obesity in older age can exacerbate bone loss.

This trial assessed the effects of higher protein intake on hip bone outcomes in 187 older adults with overweight/obesity participating in 6 months of active WL (caloric restriction + aerobic exercise) followed by a 12-month maintenance phase. Participants were randomized to either the Recommended Dietary Allowance for protein intake of 0.8 g protein/kg body weight/day (RecProt) or higher protein intake of 1.2 g protein/kg/day for the 6-month WL period only (6-mo HiProt) or the full 18-month period (18-mo HiProt). CT scans at baseline, 6 months, and 18 months were analyzed for hip volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) and cortical thickness; bone strength was assessed via finite element modeling of a sideways fall. Areal (a)BMD was measured with hip dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. Analyses examined 6-month and 18-month bone changes using analysis of covariance, and Spearman’s correlations of WL vs. bone changes.

Greater WL was associated with greater gains in hip bone strength ( p = 0.007) at 6 months, but greater trabecular vBMD loss at 18 months ( p = 0.011) and aBMD loss at 6 and 18 months ( p < 0.001). Hip bone strength increased 3.8 ± 1.7% over 6 months in the 18-mo HiProt group vs. 0.5 ± 1.6% in the RecProt group ( p = 0.02) despite similar 6-month WL across groups (−8.0 ± 5.0%); however, there were no differences between the other groups. Eighteen-month group differences were non-significant.

Higher protein intake had a beneficial effect on hip bone strength in older adults with overweight/obesity undergoing a WL intervention over the short-term.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00198-026-07845-6.
sections.introduction:
Obesity affects over one-third of older adults, but intentional weight loss (WL) is associated with bone loss and fracture risk in this population [ 1 , 2 ]. Despite WL benefits in reducing clinical consequences of obesity, musculoskeletal losses accompanying WL in older adults may exacerbate age-related osteoporosis and increase fracture risk [ 1 – 3 ]. A meta-analysis of 6 + month diet-induced WL randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults with overweight or obesity found a significant loss in hip bone mineral density (BMD), conferring a 10–15% increase in hip fracture risk [ 1 ]. While pairing exercise with diet-induced WL can attenuate BMD loss, it does not fully prevent it [ 4 ]. As bone loss does not appear to recover with weight regain [ 5 ], and may even accelerate post-WL [ 6 ], cumulative loss could potentially result in clinically meaningful increases in fracture risk [ 1 , 2 ].

WL-induced skeletal changes can be assessed by imaging metrics that serve as surrogate endpoints for fracture risk [ 7 ]. Osteoporosis and fracture prediction diagnostics traditionally rely on areal BMD (aBMD) measured with dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). However, over half of fractures occur in those with a DXA aBMD above the osteoporosis threshold [ 8 ], indicating aBMD alone cannot capture all future fracture risk. Also, DXA has limitations with obesity/WL as adipose tissue decreases aBMD accuracy [ 9 ]. Volumetric (v)BMD from quantitative computed tomography (CT) is increasingly recommended. Hip trabecular vBMD predicts fractures as well as hip aBMD in older adults, with better sensitivity to age, treatment, and obesity or WL effects [ 10 ]. Assessing trabecular and cortical vBMD separately with CT is important as both compartments uniquely contribute to bone’s mechanical structure. Further, finite element (FE) analysis of CT data is an established bioengineering technique to noninvasively estimate bone strength—a combined measure of bone morphology, compartmental vBMD, and cortical thickness that predicts fracture risk [ 11 ].

Higher protein intake during WL may attenuate bone loss [ 2 , 12 ]. Prior WL trials showed attenuated bone losses in middle-aged adults [ 13 ] and postmenopausal women [ 14 ] with overweight/obesity randomized to higher vs. lower protein diets. With 7–12% WL, total hip aBMD was 1–2% higher [ 13 , 14 ] in participants randomized to a higher protein diet. The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for protein (0.8 g protein/kg body weight/day), derived predominantly from urinary nitrogen balance studies in young adults, may underestimate protein needs in older adults to preserve bone health [ 15 , 16 ].

The objective of this older adult RCT was to determine the effects of higher protein intake (1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day), versus the RDA, on hip vBMD, cortical thickness, and bone strength during 6 months of active WL, and over an additional 12-month follow-up. We hypothesized hip vBMD, cortical thickness, and bone strength losses at 6 months would be attenuated with higher protein intake versus the RDA, and would be further attenuated in participants continuing higher protein intake over 18 months.
sections.methods:
This ancillary study leveraged the Utilizing Protein During Weight Loss to Impact Physical Function (UPLIFT) RCT ( NCT03074643 ) at Wake Forest. UPLIFT was designed to evaluate diet composition effects (e.g., protein/carbohydrate amounts) during a 6-month WL intervention and 12 months of follow-up on physical function and body composition in older adults with obesity. This 18-month, 3-arm (parallel design with equal allocation ratio across 3 arms), double-blind RCT enrolled 187 older (65–85 years), non-osteoporotic (T-scores > −2.5) men and women with obesity (body mass index 30–40 kg/m 2 or 27.0–< 30 kg/m 2 plus one risk factor [ 17 ]) who were at risk for disability (expanded Short Physical Performance Battery < 2.5) from 2017 to 2021. Exclusion criteria included WL ≥ 5%, participation in resistance training or > 20 min/day of aerobic activity in the past 6 months, or weekly alcoholic beverage consumption > 7 in women or > 14 in men. All participants provided written informed consent and a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act authorization form (IRB#000389668). Our ancillary study to the UPLIFT trial examined 6-month and 18-month intervention effects on hip volumetric BMD, cortical thickness, and bone strength assessed via CT and FE analysis (see Supplementary Figure A1 -CONSORT diagram, and full trial protocol on clinicaltrials.gov: NCT03819478 ).

All participants received a 6-month WL intervention targeting 10% body weight loss, followed by 12 months of follow-up (weight maintenance phase). Participants had their resting metabolic rate (RMR) [ 18 ] measured at baseline and at 6 months for the purpose of estimating each person’s weight maintenance calorie level. The WL intervention was designed to elicit ~ 0.5 kg/week WL with moderate caloric restriction (−500 kcal/day subtracted from each person’s estimated daily energy needs for weight maintenance at baseline) [ 19 – 21 ] and supervised moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (treadmill walking 3 days/week), meeting older adult physical activity recommendations. Exercise sessions began and ended with 3–5 min of slow walking and light stretching. Aerobic training progressed from 15 to 20 min at 50% heart rate reserve (HRR; based on age-predicted maximal heart rate) in Week 1 to 40 min at 65–70% HRR by Week 6. Treadmill speed/grade were adjusted to ensure participants exercised at their prescribed intensity. The WL intervention included nutrition education (group and individual sessions with a registered dietitian), self-monitoring skills, cognitive-behavioral strategies for lifestyle modifications, and sample meal plans with interchangeable choices. After the 6-month WL phase, there was a 12-month maintenance phase. During maintenance, participants were encouraged to maintain moderate-intensity activity (13–15 Borg’s Rating of Perceived Exertion), but resistance exercise with moderate-to-heavy weights or machines was discouraged. Participants were given a list of parks/trails and access to online aerobic videos to help maintain recommended physical activity levels. The dietitian helped each participant devise a weight maintenance strategy based on their 6-month RMR, including sample meal plans and relapse-prevention counseling. Participants also met the dietitian at a 12-month visit to review weight maintenance goals and modify as needed. Participants were counseled to consume the RDA for calcium (1200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800 IU/day) from food and supplements.

A biostatistician randomized participants to one of three isocaloric diet groups with varying protein/carbohydrate composition (Fig. 1 ) using a web-based randomization scheme with sex-stratified blocking. The RecProt group targeted the RDA for protein intake (0.8 g protein/kg body weight/day), and the two higher protein groups targeted 1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day for either the 6-month WL phase alone (6-mo HiProt) or the full 18-month trial (18-mo HiProt). Fat intake was similarly prescribed across groups (25–30% of energy; < 10% saturated fat), while carbohydrate intake fluctuated to compensate for differences in energy from protein, ensuring isocaloric diets. To achieve the higher protein dietary target in the 6-mo HiProt and 18-mo HiProt groups, participants consumed a 25 g protein supplement (NutraBio™ 100% Whey Protein Isolate) twice daily. The 50 g protein supplement contained 200 kcal, 22.6 g essential amino acids, and 10.7 g branched-chain amino acids with 5.2 g leucine, 3.0 g isoleucine, and 2.5 g valine. Since the evening meal usually has higher protein content [ 22 ], participants were instructed to consume 25 g of the supplement with their morning and midday meal/afternoon snack to optimize protein synthesis [ 23 – 25 ]. The RecProt group consumed a 25 g carbohydrate supplement twice daily (NutraBio™ CarboMax; maltodextrin, 200 kcal) to maintain blinding during the 6-month WL intervention. Supplement consumption was discontinued for the RecProt and 6-mo HiProt groups at 6 months, while the 18-mo HiProt group continued consuming the protein supplement daily during the weight maintenance phase (months 6–18). Meal plans for the weight maintenance phase were designed to match the person’s weight maintenance calorie level based on their RMR measured at 6 months. Demographic, education, and medical history were self-reported at baseline. Baseline screening by staff included height/weight to calculate BMI, the expanded Short Physical Performance Battery to select those with disability risk (scores < 2.5), and hip/spine DXA scans (Hologic Horizon A) to rule out osteoporosis (T-scores < −2.5). DXA total hip and femoral neck aBMD were measured at baseline, 6, and 18 months for the left hip unless contraindicated (e.g., hip replacement); the same hip was used in all follow-up scans. Scans were performed with manufacturer-recommended positioning and analyzed by an International Society for Clinical Densitometry-certified DXA technician blinded to the intervention group.

Weight and three 24-h dietary recalls (two weekdays; one weekend day) were obtained at baseline, 6 and 18 months. Registered dietitians conducted 24-h dietary recall interviews using Nutrition Data System for Research software from the University of Minnesota Nutrition Coordinating Center, and a validated visual portion guide to determine accurate portion sizes. Urinary nitrogen excretion over 24 h to verify protein intake [ 26 ] was measured at baseline, 6 and 18 months.

Hip vBMD, cortical thickness, and bone strength were assessed from baseline, 6-month, and 18-month CT scans. Helical scans were acquired on a Siemens SOMATOM Definition Flash dual-source CT scanner at 140 kV, 350mAs, 1-mm slice thickness, 1:1 pitch, and 0.8 s gantry speed, with a 50-cm scan field-of-view and standard abdomen reconstruction filter (Fig. 2 A). The Mindways Model 3 CT calibration phantom (Austin, TX) positioned under each participant was imaged in every scan to calibrate hip vBMD (Fig. 2 B). Monthly quality assurance was completed per manufacturer specifications. Total hip trabecular and cortical vBMD was calibrated to equivalent aqueous K 2 HPO 4 phantom densities using Mindways QCT Pro™ software. Published short-term precision reported as coefficient of variation is 0.82% for QCT hip BMD measurements [ 27 ]. The proximal femur was segmented from CT (Fig. 2 C) using semi-automated thresholding, region growing, and manual editing within Mimics (v.24, Materialise, Leuven, Belgium). Cortical thickness was measured using a cortical density-based algorithm in Stradview (University of Cambridge, UK), which is validated to have superior, sub-millimeter accuracy compared to standard thresholding [ 28 , 29 ]. Cortical thickness point clouds were cropped just below the lesser trochanter to isolate the proximal femur and calculate average femoral cortical thickness (Fig. 2 D).

Each femur CT segmentation was converted into a subject-specific tetrahedral FE mesh of uniformly-distributed nodes and elements using Ansa 20.0 (Beta CAE Systems; Root, Switzerland). Heterogenous material properties were assigned to the mesh using Enns‐Bray et al.’s approach [ 30 ] A rate-dependent non-linear MAT_FU_CHANG_FOAM (*MAT_083) material model in LS-DYNA was used for trabecular and cortical bone. Rationale for this material model is detailed in literature [ 30 ], but element deletion was not used to avoid instability after failure. Young’s modulus values calculated for the CT voxels were assigned to elements in the FE mesh using the three-dimensional interpolation material property mapping method B by Helgason et al. [ 34 , 35 ]. Using this mapping approach and published equations, the CT voxel apparent densities define the material stiffness, strain rate scaling, and yield properties of the subject-specific FE models [ 30 , 33 , 36 , 37 ].

Hip bone strength was estimated from each subject-specific FE model using a previously validated computational model set-up to simulate a sideways fall (Fig. 2 E) [ 11 , 38 ]. Each femur FE model was positioned at a 10° adduction angle and constrained at the distal end using a hinge joint located at the estimated location of the femoral condyle. The femoral head support was modeled using a spherical fit, and the greater trochanter support was modeled as a mesh offset. Both supports were rigid with no rotation and a frictionless contact at the bone interface. Simulations were performed with the LS-Dyna explicit FE solver (Ansys, Canonsburg, PA) by loading the femoral head at 1 m/s in the lateral direction, in alignment with prior experimental and computational tests of a sideways fall [ 36 , 39 ]. Bone strength was measured as the peak femoral neck section force.

Analyses conformed to intent-to-treat principles, where all participants with the CT-derived outcome measures were included in analyses according to their randomized groups. Descriptive statistics were computed overall, by intervention group at baseline, and by intervention and time at follow-up. Changes in aBMD, vBMD, cortical thickness, and bone strength measures over 6 and 18 months (on all participants who had a baseline and a 6- or 18-month follow-up CT measurement) were examined using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for age, sex, race, and baseline bone measure. The primary outcome was the 18-month change in hip trabecular vBMD, and other CT and DXA measures were secondary outcomes. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to repeat treatment effect analyses after excluding participants who discontinued the intervention, had their intervention interrupted/modified by the COVID-19 pandemic, or whose follow-up was 2–3 months out-of-window due to an in-person research pause during the pandemic (Supplemental Table A4 ). Sensitivity analyses were also conducted using linear mixed effects models (using all time points including baseline) to model changes at 6 months and 18 months, and the differences of changes among groups. Lastly, changes in bone measures were examined in relation to weight change over 6- and 18-months using Spearman’s correlations adjusted for age, race, sex, and group. Statistical analyses were conducted using SAS v9.4 and JMP Pro 17 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) with significance indicated by p < 0.025 for total hip trabecular vBMD and femoral cortical thickness (using Bonferroni correction for two primary outcomes) and p < 0.05 for all other outcomes.

The study was originally ≥ 80% powered (N = 180, 2-sided α = 0.025) to detect differences in 18-month change between groups of 0.007 g/cm 3 (SD = 0.013 g/cm 3 ) for total hip trabecular vBMD, 0.018 mm (SD = 0.032 mm) for femoral cortical thickness, and 0.037kN (SD = 0.065kN) for hip bone strength [ 40 ]. In the original power analysis, mean group differences and effect sizes at 80% power were reported for the expected 18-month sample size (N = 60/group), as well as smaller sample sizes in case of enrollment/retention shortfalls (N = 30 or 40 per group; Supplementary Table A1 ). Effect sizes ≥ 0.80 observed in prior trials have detected significant differences in hip BMD (0.80 effect size) [ 14 , 41 ] between higher versus lower protein groups, suggesting our study was adequately powered to detect differences with the enrollment and 18-month retention achieved (N = 38/group).

UPLIFT trial enrollment occurred from May 2017 to September 2020, with follow-up through April 2022. Of 187 participants enrolled, 172 had a baseline hip CT from which at least one bone outcome was measured. As described in the CONSORT diagram (Supplementary Figure A1 ), 15 participants with missing data included one participant who refused a baseline CT, 12 with hip hardware, and two with image acquisition issues. At baseline (Table 1 ), participants were aged 71.5 ± 4.3 years, 66% were women, 24% were African American, and 80% reported college/post-secondary education. Participants had obesity (34.3 ± 4.3 kg/m 2 ) and lower function (1.9 ± 0.4 expanded Short Physical Performance Battery score indicating mobility limitations with walking, balance, and/or chair stands) [ 42 ] and physical activity levels (117 ± 165 min/week self-reported moderate-intensity activity) [ 43 ]. Pre-existing conditions included diabetes (19%), prior fracture (21%), and osteopenia (9% with DXA total hip T-scores −1.0 to −1.8). Baseline characteristics in Table 1 did not differ between the treatment groups (all p > 0.05). On average, participants lost −8.0 ± 5.0% (−7.7 ± 5.2 kg) of their body weight at 6 months, and their WL was −5.0 ± 5.6% (−4.8 ± 5.5 kg) at 18 months (Supplemental Table A2 ). WL did not differ by group at 6 months (RecProt, −7.1 ± 5.2%; 6-mo HiProt, −8.5 ± 5.0%; 18-mo HiProt, −8.4 ± 4.7%) or 18 months (−4.5 ± 5.4%; −5.1 ± 5.6%; −5.3 ± 5.8%). Attendance at exercise sessions (3 days/week over 26 weeks) was similar by group (RecProt, 75.3%; 6-mo HiProt, 77.7%; 18-mo HiProt, 79.8%). As expected, dietary protein intake via 24-h dietary recall at 6 months was higher in the protein supplement groups versus the RecProt group (1.3 ± 0.4 vs. 0.8 ± 0.2 g/kg/day; p < 0.01). Dietary protein intake at 18 months was higher in the 18-mo HiProt group versus the 6-mo HiProt and RecProt groups (1.0 ± 0.4 vs. 0.8 ± 0.3 g/kg/day; p < 0.01). Similar patterns by group were observed for estimated protein intake from urinary nitrogen excretion over a 24-h period at 6 and 18 months (see Supplemental Table A2 ).

Unadjusted bone measures from baseline, 6-month, and 18-month hip CT and DXA assessments are in Supplemental Table A3 . Sub-sections below report CT and DXA-derived bone changes after adjustment for age, sex, race, and baseline bone measure.

Changes in hip trabecular vBMD (Fig. 3 ) and femoral cortical thickness did not differ by group at 6 or 18 months (Table 2 , all p > 0.05). Higher protein groups appeared to gain more trabecular vBMD over 6 months versus the RecProt group, but did not reach statistical significance. Hip bone strength increased 3.8 ± 1.7% over 6 months in the 18-mo HiProt group versus 0.5 ± 1.6% in the RecProt group ( p = 0.02; Table 2 ; Fig. 3 ), but was not significantly different from gains in the 6-mo HiProt group (2.6 ± 1.7%). sections.discussion:
In low-functioning older adults with obesity who achieved ~ 8% WL via moderate caloric restriction and moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, we found no significant group differences with higher protein intake versus the RDA for the co-primary outcomes of total hip trabecular vBMD and femoral cortical thickness at 6 or 18 months. In linear mixed effects analyses, statistically significant losses from baseline for total hip trabecular vBMD were observed at 18 months for the RecProt and 6-mo HiProt groups, but not the 18-mo HiProt group. This suggests that protein supplementation for 18 months (during active WL and the year after) may have better preserved trabecular vBMD compared to protein or carbohydrate supplementation for the 6-month WL phase. The 1–2% hip trabecular vBMD losses at 18 months in the RecProt and 6-mo HiProt groups are similar to a prior WL trial in older adults with obesity [ 40 ]. These BMD losses equate to ~ 10–20% increased risk of hip fracture [ 1 ], in contrast to a negligible risk increase in the 18-mo HiProt group. The osteoprotective effect of protein supplementation suggested by these trends also agrees with prior WL RCTs in adults with overweight/obesity, where randomization to a higher protein diet attenuated 12-month hip aBMD losses [ 13 , 14 ]. However, DXA hip aBMD group differences were non-significant in our study. While prior studies using DXA report integral hip BMD (trabecular + cortical), use of CT in this study allowed for separate assessment of intervention effects on trabecular vs. cortical compartments, as well as a composite measure of bone strength.

Group differences for secondary CT outcomes were significant only for hip bone strength at 6 months, with the 18-mo HiProt group having larger strength gains than the RecProt group ( p = 0.02). Hip bone strength gains at 6 months in the two groups randomized to higher protein were similar as expected ( p = 0.46), but the 6-mo HiProt vs RecProt group differences did not quite reach significance ( p = 0.14), possibly due to higher variability that limited statistical power. Participants continuing protein supplementation for the year after WL appeared to maintain bone strength gains > 2 times better than participants on protein supplementation for 6 months (+ 2.4% vs. + 1%), and protein supplementation in both groups may have protected against the −0.6% bone strength loss observed in the WL controls consuming the protein RDA. However, statistical significance was not achieved at the 18-month timepoint, possibly due to variability in weight maintenance amongst participants. Despite this, results suggest potential for protein supplementation during WL to reduce fracture risk as FE-derived hip bone strength predicts fracture risk better than BMD [ 11 ]. However, trochanteric soft tissue thickness (fat and muscle) likely declines with WL, and this loss of “cushioning” to attenuate forces in sideways fall may increase fracture risk despite gains in bone strength [ 44 ].

The observed 1–2% increases in cortical vBMD within all treatment groups may be due to the treadmill walking component of the intervention increasing musculoskeletal loading in this previously sedentary population. Exercise has shown beneficial skeletal effects in adults undergoing caloric restriction [ 4 , 45 ]. While resistance training is favorable for preserving bone and muscle during WL, aerobic training also shows some benefit [ 3 , 4 , 40 , 45 ]. For instance, a prior 6-month WL trial in previously sedentary postmenopausal women with overweight/obesity observed 2% gains in femoral neck BMD in those randomized to 3 days/week moderate-intensity walking (similar to UPLIFT’s exercise intervention) versus WL alone [ 46 ]. To meet UPLIFT’s exercise intensity targets, participants performed inclined treadmill walking, which is known to increase muscle activation and loading at the hip where cortical bone gains were observed [ 47 ].

Greater WL was associated with more gain in hip bone strength over 6 months. This may be attributed to the exercise component of the WL intervention increasing mechanical loading and promoting structural remodeling that increased bone strength. However, a year after discontinuing the caloric restriction and exercise intervention, there was no association between 18-month changes in weight and bone strength. Instead, greater WL was associated with more trabecular vBMD loss at 18 months, and more aBMD loss at 6 and 18 months. The extended 18-month follow-up was likely necessary to observe intervention effects on trabecular bone loss, as bone remodeling requires at least 4–6 months and can continue for 1–2 years [ 2 ].

Study strengths include the RCT design, excellent compliance for higher protein intake (especially at 6 months), long-term follow-up, and quantitative CT and DXA assessment of changes in trabecular bone, cortical bone, bone strength, and aBMD at the hip. However, there are limitations. Lack of a non-exercising control group prevents definitive testing of exercise intervention effects on bone changes observed. Further, there was no resistance training in the exercise component of the intervention, and skeletal effects of protein supplementation may be different if paired with resistance exercise, which has greater skeletal benefit than aerobic exercise. As mentioned, enrollment shortfalls and some missingness in hip CT measures reduced statistical power. Moreover, there were > 60 active participants in the intervention phase when the pandemic impacted in-person research. An in-person research pause in March–May 2020 eliminated our ability to deliver supervised group exercise and required virtual delivery of group/individual diet sessions. Phased restart of research after the pause required in-person exercise at the center to be reduced to 1–2 days/week after Week 6 of the intervention to comply with infection control measures of physical distancing, allowing fewer participants to use the shared space at the same time. The research pause led to some follow-up visits being several months out-of-window. However, our sensitivity analyses show similar results when excluding participants whose intervention or follow-up timing was impacted. Lastly, between the 6- and 18-month follow-up timepoints, over half (56%) of the participants regained > 3% of their body weight (mean ± SD: 6.9 ± 3.1%), while 29% maintained their weight (0–3% change) and 15% continued to lose weight (−3.8 ± 3.3% WL). This variability in weight change amongst participants in the year of follow-up after the intensive intervention may explain some variability in the 18-month bone changes observed.

In summary, this RCT found protein supplementation improved hip bone strength during a caloric restriction and aerobic exercise WL intervention. Future WL studies in older adults are needed to separately examine the effects of the dietary versus exercise components of the intervention on measures of bone health.
